profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This is the primary data center of the Yosemite Community College District, a public community college district in California Central Valley encompassing Modesto Junior College and Columbia College, located on the Modesto Junior College West Campus in Stanislaus County. According to the district own published capital projects documentation, the facility was built between summer 2012 and fall 2013 at a cost of approximately 7.33 million dollars, replacing an older data center the district described as having outlived its functional use. The single story building spans approximately 4,500 to 5,000 square feet and serves as the district central information technology hub supporting both Modesto Junior College and the district broader administrative systems. As a public education enterprise data center, the facility is not marketed for commercial colocation, and no third party capacity or IT megawattage figures were found. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project.

reading.body:
The Yosemite Community College District's single data center is a 4,500 to 5,000 square foot facility built in 2012-2013 for $7.33 million, designed to serve only internal instructional and administrative computing, not commercial use or third-party colocation.

Public education data centers operate under different constraints than commercial facilities. This one was built to replace aging infrastructure and to support two colleges across a Central Valley district. Its power consumption and capacity are not published, which is typical for facilities serving internal institutional needs rather than external customers. The data shows only that such centers exist as IT infrastructure across the education sector, not whether they contribute meaningfully to regional power demand or compute availability.

The absence of published megawatt figures reflects the nature of the facility. Academic data centers are built for institutional reliability and local cost control, not for scaling compute capacity. This data point does not indicate whether the district's computing needs have grown since 2013, whether the facility remains adequate, or how constrained it might be by power availability on campus. It documents that educational institutions maintain their own infrastructure, but says nothing about whether grid or building capacity limits their expansion.
